sections.html:
Columbus is the seat of Platte County in east-central Nebraska, where the Loup and Platte rivers meet. By road it is about 85 miles west-northwest of Omaha and 75 miles northwest of Lincoln. It is the eighth most populous city in the state, with 24,028 residents in 2020 and an estimated 25,248 in 2025, and it dwarfs the rest of the county: Humphrey had 905 and Newman Grove 667.

Platte County is 72.0 percent owner-occupied, with 14,094 housing units counted in 2020 and median household income of $72,335 in 2023. Median home price was $224,780 in the fourth quarter of 2024. In 2024 the county issued 71 permits for detached single-family homes and 27 for other housing units, a modest pace, so most home sales in Columbus involve existing houses rather than new builds.

sections.h2: Railroads, public power and local jobs
sections.html:
Railroads gave Columbus its start as a commercial center. Union Pacific came through in 1866, and a Burlington and Missouri River branch linked the town with Lincoln in 1881. The Loup Project canal and power plants, built from 1934 to 1938, gave it a second identity as a public-power town, and public power is still the norm. Cornhusker PPD, Elkhorn Rural PPD and Loup River PPD serve Platte County.

Farming, livestock and manufacturing lead the local economy, and Lindsay Irrigation is known worldwide for center pivot systems. Grain handling is concentrated in town, with ADM and Frontier elevators in Columbus and others in Duncan, Humphrey, Lindsay, Monroe and Tarnov. Seen from a seller's side, that means job changes and transfers can put a house on the market without much warning.

Columbus Public Schools serves about 4,100 students from preschool through grade 12. Columbus Catholic Schools unites Scotus Central Catholic High School with the St. Anthony, St. Bonaventure and St. Isidore elementary schools, and Lakeview Community Schools is also in the area. District lines do not always match city limits, so give the street address when a buyer asks which school a house feeds.

sections.h2: Which Platte County offices handle property tax
sections.html:
The Assessor, Treasurer and Register of Deeds all work from the courthouse at 2610 14th Street, Columbus, NE 68601. Courthouse hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.

  • The Assessor's page links the county's property search map.
  • The Treasurer bills and collects real estate and personal property tax.
  • The Register of Deeds records the deed that moves title.

The county's own levy in 2024 was $0.1846 per $100 of taxable valuation, which raised $13,402,589 of the $86,887,325 that all local governments levied. Taxable valuation was $7,260,726,942, so the county board's share is about 15 percent. Schools, the city and other districts add their own levies on top.

Because Columbus sits where two rivers meet, expect buyers to ask about flood exposure. The county's online map viewer includes basemap layers labeled 2019 Flood and 2020 Flood, which show what water reached in those years.

Four natural resource districts have territory in Platte County: Central Platte, Lower Elkhorn, Lower Loup and Lower Platte North. The county counts 1,297 rural drinking water wells and 2,150 irrigation wells, and any well that can pump more than 50 gallons a minute must be registered and permitted through the local district. Platte County is not zoned, so county zoning does not apply outside the incorporated towns. City zoning and building permits still apply inside Columbus.

Ask the Treasurer for the payoff on your parcel and hand it to the title company, which takes it from your proceeds. Taxes left unpaid can reach the county's tax sale, so clear a delinquent balance before it gets that far. If you are carrying an inherited or vacant house, get the balance first and decide on the sale second.

sections.h2: What a Columbus seller owes at closing
sections.html:
The seller owes Nebraska's documentary stamp tax, set under section 76-901 at $3.32 per $1,000 for transfers before 2032 and $2.32 after that.

Sellers of homes with up to four units also complete the written disclosure that section 76-2,120 requires, listing the condition of the electrical, heating, water, sewer and other systems as the seller knows them. A purchaser who is denied the statement can sue for actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and must file within one year.

  • Request a payoff letter for any loan.
  • Ask the title company to show the tax proration line by line.
  • Keep receipts for any repairs you disclosed.

faqs.q: Which county office do I contact about taxes on a Columbus house?
faqs.a: The Platte County Treasurer at the courthouse, 2610 14th Street, Columbus, NE 68601. The Treasurer bills and collects real estate and personal property tax for the county.

faqs.q: Is Platte County zoned outside Columbus?
faqs.a: No. Platte County is not zoned, though inside Columbus city zoning and building permit rules still apply.
Through public power. Cornhusker Public Power District, Elkhorn Rural Public Power District and Loup River Public Power District serve Platte County.

faqs.q: What does Nebraska deed stamp tax cost on a Columbus sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for transfers before January 1, 2032. After that date the rate drops to $2.32.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose problems when I sell a Columbus house?
faqs.a: Yes for most one-to-four-unit homes. Section 76-2,120 requires a written statement of the property's condition as the seller knows it, delivered by the time a purchase contract binds the buyer.
